title: The influence of different training load quantification methods on the fitness-fatigue model
authors: Vermeire KM, Van de Casteele F, Gosseries M, Bourgois JG, Ghijs M, Boone J
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
population: Nine subjects: 8 weeks of 3 interval sessions/week on a cycle ergometer with weekly 3-km time trials, then 3 weeks without training with weekly time trials
findings: Banister TRIMP, Lucia TRIMP, Edwards TRIMP, training stress score and session RPE were calculated for every session and each was used to fit the fitness-fatigue model.

The error relating load to performance was similar for all methods (Banister TRIMP 618 [422], Lucia TRIMP 625 [436], Edwards TRIMP 643 [465], TSS 639 [448], session RPE 558 [395], kilojoules 596 [505]).
The methods evolved differently over time, which changed the day before performance on which training has the biggest positive influence by a range of 19.6 days.
The authors concluded that load methods cannot be used interchangeably because they evolve differently.
limitations: Nine subjects, cycling, 11-week window; no running data. Single-group intervention (re-classified from experimental-crossover to other). Error units and bracket meaning are not defined in the abstract.
implications: Fix a single load metric per athlete (for example an HR-based TRIMP or session RPE with a consistent fallback) and refit model parameters if the metric or its calibration changes; do not mix metrics within one fit.
Store the load-metric identifier with each fitted parameter set so stale fits are invalidated on change.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, IJSPP, 2021. Numbers match Europe PMC abstract. Design corrected; kilojoules appears in the abstract results but not in its methods list.
